reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, tearing, and blurred vision, typically with circumcorneal (ciliary) injection rather than diffuse redness
The pupil is often small (miotic) and may be irregular if posterior synechiae have formed
Slit-lamp examination shows cells and flare in the anterior chamber; a hypopyon (layered pus) indicates severe inflammation
Keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium help characterise the inflammation as granulomatous or non-granulomatous
Strongly associated with HLA-B27 and its related systemic conditions (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis)
Management principles are topical corticosteroids to suppress inflammation and cycloplegic/mydriatic drops to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent or break synechiae
Recurrent, bilateral, or granulomatous uveitis warrants investigation for underlying systemic or infective causes
reference.pathophysiology: Anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris and ciliary body (anterior uveal tract). Breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier allows inflammatory cells and protein to leak into the anterior chamber, seen clinically as cells and flare. The process may be immune-mediated (often HLA-B27 associated or linked to systemic autoimmune disease), infective, or triggered by trauma. Inflammatory adhesions can form between the iris and lens (posterior synechiae) or the iris and trabecular meshwork (peripheral anterior synechiae), and secondary complications include raised intraocular pressure, cataract, and macular oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Acute red eye from subconjunctival haemorrhage
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to grade anterior chamber cells and flare and identify keratic precipitates
Intraocular pressure measurement to detect secondary glaucoma
Dilated fundus examination to exclude intermediate/posterior involvement and macular oedema
HLA-B27 typing and targeted systemic workup in recurrent or bilateral disease
Investigations for infective or granulomatous causes (e.g. syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis) when indicated
redFlags: Hypopyon or severe inflammation suggesting aggressive or infective uveitis, or endophthalmitis
Marked pain with a red eye and raised intraocular pressure requiring differentiation from angle closure
Bilateral, recurrent, or granulomatous disease pointing to serious systemic illness
Progressive visual loss from macular oedema or dense synechiae
reference.prognosis: Most acute, non-granulomatous, HLA-B27-associated episodes respond well to prompt topical treatment, but recurrent or chronic uveitis can lead to cataract, glaucoma, and macular oedema with lasting visual loss.
pitfalls: Prescribing topical steroids without excluding herpetic or other infective keratitis, which steroids can worsen
Failing to use a cycloplegic, allowing painful ciliary spasm and permanent posterior synechiae
Missing raised intraocular pressure or steroid-induced pressure rise during treatment
Not investigating recurrent or bilateral cases for an underlying systemic cause
management: Topical corticosteroids to suppress anterior-chamber inflammation, tapered according to response
Cycloplegic/mydriatic drops to relieve ciliary spasm and pain and to prevent or break posterior synechiae
Monitor intraocular pressure and treat secondary ocular hypertension or glaucoma, including steroid-induced pressure rise
Identify and treat any underlying systemic association (HLA-B27-related spondyloarthropathy, inflammatory bowel disease) or infective cause
Escalate refractory, chronic or bilateral disease to systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression or biologic therapy under specialist care
Surveillance for sight-threatening complications including cataract and macular oedema, with prompt ophthalmology referral for recurrent disease
